Judgment:
1.

The present is a complaint filed under section 16 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954
(Pfa Act), wherein it is alleged that the accused persons had sold misbranded food in violation of
Section 2 (ix)(k) of PFA Act read with Rule 32(e) of PFA Rules, as punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.

In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
1 2.

As per the complaint, on 25.05.2009, the food officials including Food Inspector (FI) O. P. S.
Ahalwat and Field Assistant (FA) Ashok Kumar under the supervision of Local Health Authority (LHA)/SDM Sh. Bhupinder Singh reached at the premises of M/s.

In & Out, Yashwant Place Service Station, Africa Avenue, Chanakyapuri, New Delhi-110021, where the accused no. 1 in the capacity of vendor-cum-partner of M/s. Yashwant Place Service Station was found vending "Moong Washed Dal Split" in sealed packets of 500 grams each, having identical label declaration.
The food officials lifted the sample the said food article consisting of three such sealed packets ready for sale for human consumption.
It was divided into three parts as per procedure prescribed under the PFA Act and Rules and separately packed and sealed.
Necessary documents were prepared at the spot including the vendor's receipt and panchanama.
One counterpart of the sample was deposited with the Public Analyst (PA) and remaining two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA.

Vide report dated 06.06.2009, the PA reported that the article was conforming to the standards, yet the sample was found misbranded being in violation of Rule 32(e) of PFA Rules, because there was no batch number / code number declared on the label.
Based on the report of PA, investigation was carried out by the Food Inspector as per the instructions of the SDM/LHA.
It was found that the accused no. 3 business concern M/s. Yashwant Place Service Station was a partnership firm, of which accused no. 1 and 2 were the partners.
Further, the sample article was manufactured and supplied by accused no. 4 being the proprietor of M/s. Sunny Enterprises.

Hence, after obtaining due sanction of the Director, PFA, the present complaint came to be filed against all the accused persons for violation of the section 2(ix)(k) read with Rules 32(e), as punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. Since the complaint was filed by a public servant in writing, recording of pre-summoning evidence was dispensed with and the accused persons were summoned vide order dated 20.01.2010.

Based on the report of PA, notice of accusation under section 251 CrPC was framed against all the accused persons for commission of offence under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act, vide order dated 27.04.2010, to which they pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
4. At the trial, the prosecution examined three witnesses in support of its case.

PW-1 Sh. Bhupinder Singh (SDM/LHA), PW-2 FI O. P. S. Ahalawat and PW-3 FA Ashok Kumar were the part of the team that had visited the premises of accused no. 3 and lifted the sample of "Moong Washed Dal Split"
from accused no. 1 vendor, as lying in sealed packets of 500 grams each.

These witnesses deposed about the sample proceedings conducted by them on 25.05.2009 and narrated the steps undertaken by them, including disclosing their identity, lifting three sealed packets, dividing the same in three counterparts by considering one sealed packet as one counterpart and separately packing them.

A sum of Rs. 120/- was paid to the vendor as price of the sample vide vendor's receipt Ex. PW-1/A.
Notice in Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B was prepared upon which the vendor disclosed that the food article had been purchased from accused no. 4.

Accordingly, a notice under section 14A of PFA Act Ex.
PW-1/B-1 was prepared.
Panchnama Ex. PW-1/C was also prepared and the accused issued cash memo Ex. PW-1/D while also handing over a copy of the invoice Mark-X showing purchase of commodity from accused no. 4.
The Raid Report Ex. PW-2/A was prepared at the spot.
On the next working day, one counterpart was deposited with the PA vide receipt Ex. PW-2/B and remaining two counterparts were deposited with SDM/LHA vide receipt Ex. PW-1/E.
PA report Ex. PW-1/F was received opining the sample to be misbranded.

Further investigation was carried out by PW-2 In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
2 during which various letters were written to ascertain the constitution of the business concerns involved.

Consent for prosecution Ex. PW-1/G was taken from the Director, PFA, after which the complaint Ex. PW-1/H was filed and intimation letter Ex. PW-1/I was sent to the accused vide postal receipt Ex. PW-2/E.
The witnesses were duly cross examined by the Ld. Defence Counsel, wherein they denied that the accused persons had been falsely implicated.
5. Statements of the accused persons were recorded under section 313 CrPC on 20.12.2014 wherein they denied the allegations and pleaded innocence.
They questioned the correctness of PA report and claimed that the present is a false case.
No defence evidence was however led by them.

6. It is in these circumstances, Ld. SPP for the complainant has argued that the complainant has been able to prove its case against the accused persons beyond reasonable doubt, as all the witnesses have supported its case and there is no condition in their testimony.
It is submitted that the accused has failed to rebut the findings as given by the PA.
7. On the other hand, Ld. Defence Counsel has submitted that the prosecution case fails on various grounds.

Ld. Counsel has submitted that Rule 32(e) has already been declared ultra vires of the Constitution by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in the judgement titled as Dwarka Nath v. MCD [1972 FAC 1 (SC)] and that no prosecution can lie under this provision against the accused persons.
Further, it is submitted that there are various contradictions in the testimony of the witnesses which would falsify the prosecution case.
8. I have heard the arguments advanced by Ld. SPP for the complainant and Ld. Defence Counsel for the accused persons and have carefully perused the material available on record.
9. In a criminal trial, the burden is on the complainant / prosecution to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt.
This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and has to be necessarily discharged by the prosecution itself by leading cogent and trustworthy evidence.
10. To begin with, it is seen that the accused persons have not seriously disputed the factum of lifting of sample from the premises of accused no. 3 on 25.05.2009.
It is not their case that no such proceedings took place or that no such food article was exposed / stored / meant for sale for human consumption.
All the three PWs have deposed about the sample proceedings and have narrated the steps undertaken by them in detail and in corroboration to each other.
It is not disputed that the food officials had lifted three sealed packets of 500 gm each of food article bearing identical label declaration.

11. It is then not in dispute that the premises in question belonged to accused no. 3 partnership firm,
of which accused no. 1 and 2 were the partners.
It is not in dispute that the food article had been sold by accused no. 1 in the capacity of vendor-cum-partner of accused no. 3 firm to the FI.
It is not the stand of the defence that the food article was not meant for sale or was meant for any purpose other than sale.

In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
3 12.
The accused persons have also not questioned the PA report Ex. PW-1/F on the basis of which the prosecution has been launched against them.

It is nowhere the stand of the accused persons that the said report is wrong or any incorrect method had been applied by the PA, primarily because the said report is in their favour in as much as the sample was found conforming to the prescribed standards as to its nature, quality and substance.
13.
It is also seen that the accused persons have not questioned the observation of the PA that the sample was without declaration of batch number.
It is nowhere the stand of the accused persons that the said observation was wrong or that some batch number / code number in compliance of Rule 32(e) of PFA Rules had been mentioned on the label.

The FI had reproduced the contents of the label on Form VI Ex. PW-1/B which was duly signed by the vendor /accused no. 1 and it can be seen that there is no lot number or code number or batch number mentioned therein.

It is nowhere the stand of the accused persons that the FI had incorrectly or incompletely mentioned the label declarations on Ex. PW-1/B or had deliberately omitted to mention the batch number thereupon.

No attempt was made by the accused persons to call for the original label from the office of the PA,
when this option was also available, in case they were to take stand that batch number was there.
Even in their statements under section 313 CrPC, the accused persons never claimed that any batch number was there on the label or that the PA report was wrong on this point.

14. Accused no. 1, 2 and 3 have claimed that they had purchased sealed packets of the sampled commodity from M/s Sunny Enterprises (proprietorship concern of accused no. 4) vide bill no.
H00238 dated 14.05.2009.
This fact was disclosed by the vendor even at the time of sampling and also mentioned on Form-VI Ex. PW-1/B by the vendor, with specific details of the bill.
The vendor had also furnished copy of the said bill to the FI.
Even the label declaration on the sampled product would clearly show that the food article had been "Packed and Marketed by M/s. Sunny Enterprises.
The label of the product bore complete particulars and address of the said business concern.
15. No objection has been raised by accused no. 4 as to her association with the said business concern.
It is nowhere her case that she was not the proprietor of M/s. Sunny Enterprises.
It is not here stand that the business concern was not a proprietorship concern or that some other person was in charge of or responsible for its affairs.
She has not taken a stand anywhere that the bill furnished by accused no. 4 was a forged or fabricated document.
She never claimed that the food article was not packed or marketed by her business concern or was not supplied by her to the accused no. 3 firm or had been supplied to any other person.
She has never questioned the correctness of the bill in question.
She never took stand that the food article might have been purchased by accused no. 3 from some other supplier or distributor.
She has not claimed that the food article was a duplicate or spurious food article being falsely sold in her name.

For that matter, it is strange to observe that all the accused persons were represented at the trial by the same set of lawyers, despite the fact that the interests of accused no. 1, 2 and 3 on one hand, are at conflict with the interests of accused no. 4 on the other hand.

If the accused no. 1, 2 and 3 are able to show that the food article had been purchased by them from the accused no. 4 supplier against a proper bill /
invoice / cash memo and further that the food article had been sold by them in the same state as purchased, then they are entitled to the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act and in that case, the liability would only fall upon the accused no. 4.

Similarly, if they fail to establish such In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
4 ingredients, then accused no. 4 may seek her exoneration.
Despite such conflicting interests, all the accused persons continued to be represented by the same counsel and even the witnesses were cross
-examined jointly.

16. In the present case, accused no. 1, 2 and 3 maintained that the food article had been supplied by accused no. 4 and this fact has not been controverted either by the prosecution or by accused no. 4.

The fact that the complaint was filed against accused no. 4, would establish that the FI was satisfied that the food article had been purchased by accused no. 1, 2 and 3 from accused no. 4 vide the bill dated 14.05.2009.
The FI did not find anything during investigation that could controvert this stand.
The FI must have been sure that the product lifted by him was a part of the supplies made to accused no. 1, 2 and 3 vide this bill.
Otherwise, there was no occasion to implicate the accused no. 4 in the present matter.
And this fact has not been denied by any of the accused persons.

It is nowhere the stand of any of the accused persons that the food article had been purchased by accused no. 1, 2 and 3 from any other distributor / manufacturer or from the same manufacturer but vide a different bill.
No such stand had been taken by the accused persons either during the trial or in their statements under section 313 CrPC.
There is no rebuttal anywhere even during the cross-examination of the witness that the food article had been purchased by accused no. 1, 2 and 3 vide bill dated 14.05.2009.

It is further an admitted fact that the food article as lifted by the food officials was in originally sealed condition as was purchased by the vendor from the supplier and therefore, was being sold in the same state as purchased.

17. It is to be noted that as per section 14 of PFA Act, no manufacturer or distributor or dealer in any article of food shall sell such article to any vendor unless he also gives a warranty in writing about the nature or quality of such article to the vendor.

In the year 1976, a Proviso was added to this section, to the effect that the bill, cash memorandum or invoice in respect of sale of any article of food given by a manufacturer or distributor or dealer in such article to the vendor thereof shall be deemed to be a warranty given by such manufacturer, distributor or dealer.

Therefore, the moment a particular invoice / bill is proved to be correct with respect to any food article, and it is established that the article was being sold in the same state as purchased, the vendor would get the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of the PFA Act.
18.
In the present case, it has been established that the food article had been purchased by accused no.1, 2 and 3 from accused no. 4 against the bill no. H00238 dated 14.05.2009.
It is nowhere the case of anyone that the food was not being sold in the same state as purchased.
As such, the said vendors are protected under the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act and no case would be made out against them.
19. As far as the accused no. 4 is concerned, she has never disputed the fact that there was no batch number mentioned on the label of the food article, as alleged by the prosecution.

As stated earlier, it is not her case that the FI had incorrectly or incompletely mentioned the label declarations on Ex.
PW-1/B or had deliberately omitted to mention the batch number thereupon.
It is not her case that the label found on the samples had been changed by any third party or there was any foul play in the same.
It is not her stand that the article sold by her was not being sold in the same condition by the vendors as was purchased from her.

In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
5 20.

It is however argued by Ld. Defence Counsel that the accused has not received the intimation letter with PA report and thus, her right under section 13(2) to get the sample analysed through the CFL, got frustrated, as held in precedents titled as Rameshwar Dayal v. State of UP [1996(2) PFA Cases 197] and State of Orissa v. Gouranga Sahu [2002 (2) FAC 110] wherein it has been laid down that the right under section 13(2) PFA Act is valuable right and it is the duty of the complainant to ensure that such right is not frustrated.
21.

entities.text: Rameshwar Dayal v. State of UP [1996(2) PFA Cases 197]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: State of Orissa v. Gouranga Sahu [2002 (2) FAC 110]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: As per the scheme of the Act, after a sample (in three counterparts) is lifted by the FI, he is required as per section 11 to send, by the immediately succeeding working day, one counterpart of sample to PA for analysis and deposit the remaining two counterparts with the LHA.
The PA analyses the sample and delivers report to the LHA under section 13 of Act.

Under section 13(2) of the Act, after institution of prosecution against the accused, the LHA is required to forward a copy of the PA report to the accused, informing that he may apply to the Court, within 10 days of receipt of report, for getting the sample (second counterpart) analysed by CFL.
Thus, this provision mandates sending of PA report to the accused by the LHA.
It is a settled law that if the report is not so sent, it would cause prejudice to the accused and his right cannot be frustrated by the prosecution.
The point to be noted is, that such forwarding of report has to be after the institution of the prosecution in the court and not prior to filing of the case.
Also, the accused has 10 days time from the date of receipt of report to apply to the court.

Again, if so applied, the court requires the LHA to produce counterpart of the sample before it, and upon receipt of such requisition, LHA is required to produce it within 5 days (section 13(2-A) of Act) before the court.
The court then sends the said counterpart to the CFL for analyses, and the Director, CFL is required to send report of analysis within 1 month.
22. Well, in my considered view, there is no merit in the contention that the PA report was not received by the accused.
PW-1 and PW-2 deposed about sending the copy of PA report with intimation letter through registered post vide receipt Ex. PW-2/E.
The evidence also shows that the original postal registration receipts had been produced in the court to this extent during the evidence of PW-2.

Therefore, it cannot be said that the document was not proved, primarily because no objection was raised by the defence as to the factum of sending the letter to or receipt thereof by the accused at the trial.
No suggestion was given to any PWs that no such receipt was in existence.
It is not the case where no original receipt exists.

Not even a single suggestion was given to the witnesses that the postal receipt Ex. PW-2/E was a forged or fabricated document or that no such letter was sent or that it was sent at an incorrect address.
The accused no. 4 has never disputed the factum of sending the letter through registered post at the trial.
No witness was asked to rebut any such proposed defence and it was only at the fag end of the matter during her statement under section 313 CrPC that she claimed that no letter was received by her.
Such a stand is apparently an afterthought.
Thus, accused no. 4 cannot take benefit on this count and on the basis of evidence, it is clear that the letter had been sent to her.
23. Once this fact is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.
It is not the case of the accused that the said letter was sent at an incorrect address.
No such stand has been taken by the accused no. 4 at any stage of trial including prosecution evidence, statement of accused or defence evidence.

In such a position, when a letter had been sent through registered post In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
6 at a correct and proper address, there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.

The burden would not upon be the complainant to show delivery of the letter and such burden would now shift upon the accused to show that the letter was not so delivered to her despite having been sent at a correct address through registered post.
But the accused has not led any evidence to this effect.
No attempt was made by her to summon the records of postal department to show as to whom the letter was delivered or if it remained undelivered.
There is no evidence to show that the letter was not delivered to the accused no. 4.
Accused has not claimed that she was not staying at that address or was staying at some other address or that it could not have been served upon her at the relevant time.
It is not her claim that she was not available at the said address or had shifted from that address.
Thus, accused no. 4 has failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
The burden would be upon the accused to prove anything to the contrary.
By not leading any evidence to support her stand, the version of the accused no. 4 remains unsubstantiated.
Therefore, it has to be held that the intimation letter and PA report were delivered upon the accused no. 4 in due course.
The accused cannot therefore opt to simply deny the things and claim that PA report was not received by her.

24. Therefore, it cannot be said that the complaint had frustrated her right under section 13(2) PFA Act.
25.
Even otherwise, technically, to establish the offence of misbranding, analysis of food article by the PA or even CFL would not be required.

Public Analyst is a chemical expert who is primarily required to chemically analyse a sample of food article lifted by the FI to determine its analytical values and then to give opinion as to if the food article was adulterated or if it was not conforming to the prescribed standards.
Such chemical and scientific analysis is required to ascertain the ingredients and chemical composition of the food article.

As far as the offence of misbranding is concerned, it pertains to label declarations on the package of the food article and no chemical analysis of the product is ordinarily required to establish if the article is misbranded or not.

There might be situations where it is necessary to ascertain the chemical composition of the product to ascertain if the ingredients of the product are in conformity with the label declarations on the product.

But in other cases where the label declarations themselves are not as per the prescribed rules, no chemical analysis of the product would be necessary to establish whether the product is misbranded or not.

26. Whenever a sample is lifted by the FI, as per the procedure established under the PFA Act and Rules, the same is required to be divided into three parts and then, one counterpart is to be sent to PA for analysis and the remaining two counterparts are to be deposited with the LHA.
The PA is required to chemically analyse the sample and then give opinion not only on the point of adulteration but also as to misbranding.

Even if a sample is misbranded on the face of it, it is still required to be sent to the PA for chemical analysis, so as to ascertain if it is in compliance or violation of the rules, including those pertaining to prescribed standards as to its nature, substance and quality as well as those pertaining to labelling and packaging standards.

27. However, in cases where the product conforms to the standards and there is no adulteration therein, and the ingredients of the product are also as per the label declaration, the chemical In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
7 analysis and composition of the product need not be gone into to ascertain if the product is otherwise misbranded.
For that, the court (or any other person for that matter) is only required to have a bare look at the label declarations on the product and then determine if such declarations are as per the rules.

Irrespective of opinion of the PA as to misbranding on the basis of label declarations simplicitor, the court is not bound by any such opinion, primarily because the same is not based on any chemical tests or analytical values arrived at after scientific analysis.

28. If the court is only required to peruse the label declarations appearing on the package of a food article and not to go into the chemical analysis or composition of the same, any irregularity in the sample proceedings or in the chemical analysis by the PA, which has no effect on the label declarations, would not give any benefit to the accused.

To establish misbranding simplicitor, any opinion of a chemical expert is neither required nor relevant, though in every case where a sample is lifted by the FI, it is necessary to send it to PA for chemical analysis to ascertain if it is in conformity of PFA Act and Rules.

29. Similarly, if a sample is sent to the Central Food Laboratory (CFL) upon the accused exercising his right under section 13(2) of PFA Act, only the analytical values therein would be final and conclusive in terms of section 13(3) and 13(5) of PFA Act and not the observations as to the labelling standards.
If the label declarations are independent of chemical analysis by the PA or CFL, the analytical findings given by them need not be looked into to determine the offence of misbranding.

The court is required to arrive at its decision to find out if the sample is misbranded or not, by carefully perusing by contents of the label on the package of the food article, without being influenced by the analytical values arrived by the PA or CFL after chemical analysis.

30. It follows that even if there is some irregularity in the procedure adopted for lifting the sample or in the tests performed by the chemical analysts, that would not be a reason to conclude that the sample was not misbranded.

Any irregularity in lifting of the sample or its analysis might be relevant and have material bearing on the opinion of the chemical experts as far as the analytical details are concerned, on the basis of which the experts may opine if sample is adulterated or substandard, but when the issue is not with respect to any adulteration and only of non- compliance of packaging and labelling rules independent of such chemical analysis, the court need not even look into the opinion given by the PA or even CFL in their reports, unless of course the irregularity or illegality goes to the root of the matter.

Thus, even if the right of the accused under section 13(2) PFA Act is accepted to be frustrated (though there is nothing to establish any such defence), that would not give any benefit to the accused as the court is not concerned with any such analytical values of chemical experts and has to confine itself only to the label declarations on the product.
31. Ld. Defence Counsel has then pointed some contradictions in the evidence by the witnesses.
It is informed that as per PW-1, they left from their office at 12.00/12.30 PM, but PW-3 stated that they left from their office at 08.25 PM.
Similarly, PW-2 and PW-3 stated that it took about one hour at the spot but PW-1 stated that he remained there for about 35 minutes.
32. Well, in my considered view, these are very minor contradictions which do not go to the root of the matter.

Minor contradictions, variations and improvements do creep in the testimony of the In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
8 witnesses with the passage of time but unless such contradictions are material enough to go to the root of the matter, they cannot be allowed to be negate the prosecution case on all other counts.

entities.text: In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: If the witnesses are otherwise truthful and their testimony is creditable, minor contradiction would not negate their version on all the other counts.
Human memory is liable to fade with the passage of time and witnesses cannot be expected to remember all minute details of the incident after expiry of long period.
In the present case, the sample was lifted on 25.05.2009 and the witnesses were examined in the year 2012/2013.
Minor contradictions therefore cannot be ruled out.
33. Thus, PW-3 is apparently wrong when he stated that they left from office at 08.25 PM, as the sample had been lifted in morning.

PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 corroborated the version of each other by informing that about 3 to 4 persons were present and they requested 2-3 public persons to join as a witness in the sample proceedings but they refused.

PW-1 and PW-2 corroborated each other by informing that sealing material was with the FA but the contradictory statement of PW-3 that the material was with the FI would not negate the entire prosecution case being not material.
PW-2 and PW-3 similarly stated that it took about one hour at the spot and therefore, the version of PW-1 that he remained there for about 35 minutes would be only a minor variation.
All the material particulars including steps taken by them in lifting of sample, division of sample, execution of necessary documents etc. is corroborative and trustworthy.

34. As far as Rule 32(e) is concerned, the defence has relied upon the judgement titled as Dwarka Nath v. MCD (supra) wherein the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India had struck down the said provision being beyond the rule making power under section 23(1) of the PFA Act.
I have gone through the said judgement as well as the applicable rules.
However, in my considered view, this judgement would not apply to the present case.

35. In the said judgement, the decisive factors as observed by the Hon'ble Court can be noticed as under:
(a) There was no definition of the expression "batch number" or "code number" in the Act or in the Rules.

No affidavit had been filed on behalf of respondent to show whether any technical meaning in the trade was given to these expressions and the matter was based only on the evidence of the Food Inspector.

(b) No notification issued by the Central Government had been brought to the notice of the Hon'ble court with respect to the food article in question showing the applicability of Section 23(1)(c) of PFA Act.

(c) As per Rule 32(e) [as it is existed at that time (the said judgement was passed on 23.04.1971)], "batch number or code number", had to be mentioned in Hindi or English or numericals or alphabets or in combination, on every label.

36. In view of this factual position, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held that:
In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
9

(a) There was nothing in clauses (c), (f) and (g) of section 23(1) of PFA Act which would give power to the Central Government to frame rules requiring the batch number or code number to be given on the labels, particularly there was no notification brought to the notice of the Hon'ble Court under clause (c).

(b) Clause (d) of section 23 (1) would also not be applicable as there was no rational or remote connection between the batch or code number artificially given by a packer and the public or the purchaser being prevented from being deceived or misled as to the character, quality or quantity of the article, contained in a sealed tin.

(c) As there is no definition of the expression "batch number" or "code number"
either in the Act or the Rules, and it was admitted that even where batch or code number was to be given, there was no further obligation to specify in the label the date of packing and manufacture of the article of food or the period within which the article of food had to be utilised, used or consumed, merely giving an artificial batch number or code number will not be of any use to the public or to the purchaser.
Hence, Rule 32(e) was held to be beyond the rule-making power even under section 25(1)(d) of the Act.

Defence Counsel has also pointed out that relying upon the said judgement of Dwarka Nath v. MCD, Hon'ble High Court of Delhi has also upheld the acquittal of an accused in Criminal LP no.
17/2009 filed against the judgement dated 24.01.2009 of the Ld. ASJ-01 (South), Patiala House Courts, New Delhi in Criminal Appeal no. 34/08.

entities.label: COURT

It is submitted that against the said judgement of the Hon'ble High Court of Delhi, the State went in appeal before the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case titled as NCT of Delhi v. sentences.text: A careful study of the position would however, negate the stand taken by the Ld. Defence Counsel.

It is to be noted that there has been a lot of difference in the language of Rule 32(e) as it existed at the time when the judgement of Dwarka Nath v. MCD was passed and that as it existed on the day when the sample was lifted and as it existed till the PFA Act was repealed and substituted by new Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006.
20. It is to be noted that after 1971, when the judgement of Dwarka Nath v. MCD was passed holding Rule 32(e) as ultra vires of the Constitution, the said rule was amended.

This Rule 32 was last amended in 2006 and clauses (d), (e), (f), (g) and (h) of Rule 32 were substituted by G.S.R. 491(E)
dated 21.08.2006 (w.e.f 20.02.2008) as corrected by G.S.R. 518(E) dated 31.07.2007.
38.

At the time of Dwarka Nath v. MCD judgement, Rule 32(e) read as: "a batch number or code number either in Hindi or English numericals or alphabets or in combination".
39. Rule 32(e) as it is existed prior to the G.S.R. 491(E) read as: "a distinctive batch number or lot number or code number, either in numericals or alphabets or in combination, the numericals or In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
10 alphabets or their combination, representing the batch number or lot number or code number being preceded by the words "Batch No.", or "Batch, or Lot No.", or "Lot" or any distinguishing prefix."

40 . Rule 32(e) as it stood on the day of sampling in the present case read as: "Lot/Code/Batch Identification- A Batch number or Code number or Lot number which is a mark of identification by which the food can be traced in the manufacture and identified in the distribution, shall be given on the label".
41.

An apparent distinction, which can be seen in the language of Rule 32(e) as it existed earlier and its existed at the time of sampling, is that the purpose of giving batch number / code number / lot number has been specified, that is to identify the food article by any identification mark so as to enable it to be traced in the manufacturing and distribution process.
Such meaning / purpose was earlier missing from the language of Rule 32(e).

42. Therefore, in view of the present language of Rule 32(e), it cannot be said that there is no definition of these expressions in the Act or in the Rules so as to reveal their purpose, as observed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in Dwarka Nath v. MCD decided in 1971.
The purpose of mentioning such batch number / code number/ lot number has now been made clear by the legislature.
23. It cannot be said now that a purchaser would not have any concern with the batch number or code number or lot number on the label artificially given by the manufacturer / packer.

It is to be understood that if such a separate number is given to various lots of products prepared, it would be possible to trace the manufacturer/supplier/dealer and to fix their liability for selling adulterated or misbranded food.
Under PFA Act, not only the seller but distributors / supplier and manufacturers are also liable for prosecution.

Therefore, unless it is established that any particular product lifted from the vendor was purchased from a particular supplier/ distributor, it shall not be possible to apprehend any such person and fix his responsibility.

In the absence of any such mark of identification, it would be very easy for any distributor/supplier to deny/disown the lifted incriminating food product to be the one sold by him through a particular invoice.
43. It is necessary to be noticed that as per section 14 of PFA Act, every manufacturer or distributor or dealer as to sell an article of food by giving a warranty in writing in the prescribed form.

As per section 19(2) of PFA Act, a vendor can seek the benefit of warranty if he is able to prove that he had purchased the article of food from any manufacturer, distributor or dealer with a written warranty in the prescribed form.

Rule 12-A of PFA Rules provide that every manufacturer, distributor or dealer selling the article of food to a vendor shall give either separately or in the bill, cash memo or label, a warranty in Form-VI-A.
Therefore, to get warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act, every such vendor or supplier has to establish that he was having a written warranty conforming to Rule 12-A and Form VI-A as prescribed.
This becomes necessary so as to identify the product as lifted by the food officials.

If a vendor has been purchasing a particular food article from the distributor/supplier continuously in routine course for a long time, it is only through the batch number or code number mentioned on the article that it could be established as to by what bill/invoice the said product was purchased.

In the absence of any such batch number or code In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
11 number having been mentioned on the bills and the products, it would be ordinarily difficult for the food officials to identify if the product lifted for sampling is the same product as was sold to the vendor vide any particular bill or any bill prior thereto or any bill of some other supplier.
44. At this stage, it is also to be seen that the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India had held Rule 32(e) as it existed at that time, ultra vires.
Thus, upon passing of the said judgement, Rule 32(e) no more existed in the eyes of law.

However, when Rule 32(e) in modified language was again inserted and then substituted with a different language at its exists now, such a provision cannot be said to have been declared ultra vires merely because the number of Rule 32(e) is the same.

There is force in the stand of Ld. SPP for the complainant that Rule 32(e) which had been declared ultra vires, has now been completely changed and the modified Rule 32(e) as it existed when the sample was lifted has never been declared unconstitutional by any court of law.
The said provision inserted / substituted by G.S.R. 491(E) as corrected by G.S.R. 518(E) has to be considered as valid unless declared unconstitutional by any court.
45. In view of this position, judgement in Dwarka Nath v. MCD would not help the accused.

For that matter, even the order dated 27.08.2015 passed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court of India in case titled as NCT of Delhi v. Mohinder Singh [Criminal Appeal no. 1470/2011] would not be applicable,
because that order also pertained to a sample lifted on 23.08.1993 (copy of the pleadings to this effect has been shown by the Ld. Defence Counsel).

sentences.text: Since Rule 32(e) stood amended and substituted in 2006 /2007, the said Rule would be applicable to the present case where the sample was lifted on 25.05.2009.
The said rule has not been declared unconstitutional or ultra virus and is therefore binding.

26. No explanation has been given as to why no batch number had been given by the accused no. 4 on the label of the food article while all other declarations had been given as per the PFA Act and Rules.
Therefore, there is clear violation of Rule 32(e) in the present case, which makes out violation of section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act, as punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
46. No other stand has been taken by the accused no. 4 at the trial or during the arguments advanced.
47. In view of this discussion, it can be said that the complainant / prosecution has been able to establish its case and prove the guilt of the accused no. 4 beyond the shadow of reasonable doubt.

It has been proved that the accused no. 4 had sold / distributed / manufactured a misbranded food in violation of section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act read with Rule 32(e) of PFA Rules, and has committed the offence punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
The other accused persons are entitled to the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of the PFA Act 48.
Having said so, the accused no. 4 is held guilty and convicted for the offence punishable under section 16(1)(a) of the PFA Act.
Other accused persons are acquitted of the charges.

Their bail bonds shall remain in force for the next six months in terms of section 437-A, CrPC.
49.
Let the matter be listed for arguments on sentence qua the convicted accused no. 4.

This burden cannot be shifted to the accused and has to be necessarily discharged by the prosecution itself by leading cogent and trustworthy evidence.
It is not the stand of the defence that the food article was not meant for sale or was meant for any purpose other than sale.

invoice / cash memo and further that the food article had been sold by them in the same state as purchased, then they are entitled to the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act and in that case, the liability would only fall upon the accused no. 4.
The fact that the complaint was filed against accused no. 4, would establish that the FI was satisfied that the food article had been purchased by accused no. 1, 2 and 3 from accused no. 4 vide the bill dated 14.05.2009.
In the present case, it has been established that the food article had been purchased by accused no.1, 2 and 3 from accused no. 4 against the bill no. H00238 dated 14.05.2009.
It is nowhere the case of anyone that the food was not being sold in the same state as purchased.
As such, the said vendors are protected under the benefit of warranty under section 19(2) of PFA Act and no case would be made out against them.
19. As far as the accused no. 4 is concerned, she has never disputed the fact that there was no batch number mentioned on the label of the food article, as alleged by the prosecution.
23. Once this fact is so established, section 27 of the General Clauses Act would come into play.

In such a position, when a letter had been sent through registered post In Re vs A-1) Raj Kumar Goel on 7 December, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/19966618/
6 at a correct and proper address, there would be a presumption of service under section 27 of the General Clauses Act in favour of the complainant.
The burden would not upon be the complainant to show delivery of the letter and such burden would now shift upon the accused to show that the letter was not so delivered to her despite having been sent at a correct address through registered post.
Thus, accused no. 4 has failed to rebut the presumption under section 27 of the General Clauses Act.
The burden would be upon the accused to prove anything to the contrary.
Such chemical and scientific analysis is required to ascertain the ingredients and chemical composition of the food article.
As far as the offence of misbranding is concerned, it pertains to label declarations on the package of the food article and no chemical analysis of the product is ordinarily required to establish if the article is misbranded or not.
Even if a sample is misbranded on the face of it, it is still required to be sent to the PA for chemical analysis, so as to ascertain if it is in compliance or violation of the rules, including those pertaining to prescribed standards as to its nature, substance and quality as well as those pertaining to labelling and packaging standards.
Irrespective of opinion of the PA as to misbranding on the basis of label declarations simplicitor, the court is not bound by any such opinion, primarily because the same is not based on any chemical tests or analytical values arrived at after scientific analysis.
To establish misbranding simplicitor, any opinion of a chemical expert is neither required nor relevant, though in every case where a sample is lifted by the FI, it is necessary to send it to PA for chemical analysis to ascertain if it is in conformity of PFA Act and Rules.
If the witnesses are otherwise truthful and their testimony is creditable, minor contradiction would not negate their version on all the other counts.
Human memory is liable to fade with the passage of time and witnesses cannot be expected to remember all minute details of the incident after expiry of long period.

Under PFA Act, not only the seller but distributors / supplier and manufacturers are also liable for prosecution.
Therefore, unless it is established that any particular product lifted from the vendor was purchased from a particular supplier/ distributor, it shall not be possible to apprehend any such person and fix his responsibility.
In the absence of any such mark of identification, it would be very easy for any distributor/supplier to deny/disown the lifted incriminating food product to be the one sold by him through a particular invoice.
If a vendor has been purchasing a particular food article from the distributor/supplier continuously in routine course for a long time, it is only through the batch number or code number mentioned on the article that it could be established as to by what bill/invoice the said product was purchased.
However, when Rule 32(e) in modified language was again inserted and then substituted with a different language at its exists now, such a provision cannot be said to have been declared ultra vires merely because the number of Rule 32(e) is the same.
The said provision inserted / substituted by G.S.R. 491(E) as corrected by G.S.R. 518(E) has to be considered as valid unless declared unconstitutional by any court.
The said rule has not been declared unconstitutional or ultra virus and is therefore binding.
Therefore, there is clear violation of Rule 32(e) in the present case, which makes out violation of section 2(ix)(k) of PFA Act, as punishable under section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act.
